title: Managing a Classroom Activity
scenario: You are teaching an English lesson to a primary school class. The pupils are going to practise reading short sentences from their textbooks. Your task is to organise the activity, give clear instructions, manage turn-taking and keep everyone involved.

steps.title: Getting Started with the Textbook
opening: The lesson has already begun. The pupils are sitting at their desks with their English textbooks in front of them.
You are going to use an exercise on page 75. Some pupils have their books open, while others are still waiting for instructions.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils open their textbooks and find page 75.

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: I've found it!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Most pupils are looking at the correct page.

choices.feedback: The instruction directs everyone to the required textbook page.

reaction.speaker: class
reaction.text: Yes!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several pupils look towards you, but their textbooks are still closed.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to page 75 on the board. The pupils find the page.

choices.feedback: Checking readiness does not tell pupils which page to open.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils stand up beside their desks.

reaction.speaker: alex
reaction.text: Are we going to do something standing up?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You indicate that they can sit down and show them page 75 on the board.

choices.feedback: Standing up is unrelated to opening the textbook.

transition: Everyone is now sitting with their textbooks open at page 75.
The exercise contains several short sentences. The first part requires the whole class to read together.

steps.title: Reading Together
opening: The pupils look at the first sentence. Some are already preparing to read it, while others are waiting for your instruction.
You want everyone to read the sentence at the same time.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Maria raises her hand.

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: I know!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Other pupils also begin raising their hands. They expect an individual question.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the sentence and gesture for everyone to read together.

choices.feedback: Asking for an answer invites individual participation, not shared reading.

reaction.speaker: class
reaction.text: We like English!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils read the first sentence together.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Most of them follow the same rhythm.

choices.feedback: The phrase clearly asks the whole class to read simultaneously.

choices.text: Come to the front of the class.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Alex looks around and stands up.

reaction.speaker: alex
reaction.text: Me, teacher?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You indicate that he can stay seated and point to the sentence for everyone to read.

choices.feedback: Coming to the front does not ask everyone to read together.

transition: The class completes the first sentence together.
You move to the second sentence. The pupils begin reading, but several of them are speaking very softly.

steps.title: Speaking Clearly
opening: The pupils are reading the second sentence together. Their pronunciation is understandable, but the voices of the pupils at the back are very quiet.
You want everyone to repeat the sentence more loudly.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils repeat the complete sentence, but their voices are still rather quiet.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You gesture for them to speak louder, and they repeat it once more.

choices.feedback: A complete sentence is useful, but the issue is speaking too quietly.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils stop reading immediately.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several look towards you, waiting to understand why the activity has stopped.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the sentence and gesture for them to continue more loudly.

choices.feedback: Stopping the reading prevents the activity instead of improving volume.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils repeat the sentence in louder voices.

reaction.speaker: class
reaction.text: We like our school!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You can now hear the class clearly.

choices.feedback: The instruction directly requests louder reading.

transition: The pupils finish the group-reading part of the exercise.
The next part requires pupils to read individually. The class has already practised taking turns in previous lessons.

steps.title: Taking Turns
opening: The pupils look at the next short paragraph.
They know that each pupil will read a few sentences before the next person takes a turn.
You want to find out whose turn it is to read.
steps.question: What would you say?

choices.text: Whose turn is it to read?

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: It's Anna's turn!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna looks at her book and prepares to read the paragraph.

choices.feedback: This asks precisely whose turn it is in the reading order.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Alex raises his hand.

reaction.speaker: alex
reaction.text: I know the answer!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several pupils look at the text, expecting a question.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Maria reminds the class that Anna is next in the reading order.

choices.feedback: This seeks a correct answer instead of identifying the next reader.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several pupils begin reading the paragraph together.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna pauses because she was expecting to read individually.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You signal for the class to stop and indicate that Anna should read first.

choices.feedback: Whole-class reading conflicts with taking individual turns.

transition: Anna begins reading the paragraph. She reads steadily, and most pupils follow the text.
After a few sentences, Alex starts whispering to Maria. Anna continues reading but seems slightly distracted.

steps.title: Keeping the Class Focused
opening: Anna is reading aloud at the front of the classroom. Alex is talking quietly to Maria instead of listening.
You want Alex to pay attention to Anna without unnecessarily interrupting her reading.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Alex stops speaking.

reaction.speaker: alex
reaction.text: Sorry.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: He looks towards you briefly, then returns his attention to the text.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna continues reading.

choices.feedback: This stops the conversation, but does not direct attention to Anna.

choices.text: Listen to what Anna is saying.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Alex stops whispering and looks towards Anna.

reaction.speaker: alex
reaction.text: Okay, teacher.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna continues reading without further interruption.

choices.feedback: The instruction redirects Alex to listen to the pupil who is reading.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several pupils join Anna and begin reading aloud.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna stops for a moment, unsure whether she should continue alone.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You indicate that the other pupils should listen while Anna finishes the paragraph.

choices.feedback: The command makes everyone read and interrupts Anna’s individual turn.

transition: Anna finishes reading the paragraph. You acknowledge her work, and the class turns to the next part of the exercise.
The pupils have completed the reading task and are ready for a new activity on the same page.

steps.title: Moving to the Next Activity
opening: The reading activity is complete. The next exercise contains short questions about the text.
You want to move the class to the next activity without repeating the previous instructions.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils look at the next exercise.

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: Exercise two?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You nod. The pupils begin reading the questions.

choices.feedback: This moves pupils to the next exercise.

reaction.speaker: class
reaction.text: Yes!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils wait for a more specific instruction.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the next exercise, and they begin working.

choices.feedback: Readiness alone does not tell pupils which activity comes next.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The classroom is already quiet.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The pupils remain seated and wait for instructions.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the next exercise to show what they should do.

choices.feedback: The pupils are already quiet, so this delays the next task.

final: The pupils move on to the comprehension questions. Most are following the activity independently, and you begin checking their answers.
